**Visual observations:**
- Young soybean seedling, very early stage (just above soil line)
- Plant has completely collapsed and died — leaves are dry, brown, papery, and curled
- Stem appears constricted/damaged near the soil line
- No water-soaked tissue visible; the collapsed tissue is dry and firm-looking
- Healthy plants visible in the background, indicating localized damage

**Reasoning:**
The key features here are: (1) seedling collapse at the soil line, (2) dry, brown, papery dead tissue (not water-soaked or soft), and (3) the damage is focused at/below the soil line. This dry canker pattern at the hypocotyl is the hallmark of **Rhizoctonia**. 

- **Pythium** causes water-soaked, soft rot — tissue would be mushy, not dry/papery.
- **Phytophthora** in young plants causes soft rot collapse as well.
- **Rhizoctonia** causes reddish-brown, sunken, **firm and dry** lesions on the hypocotyl at the soil line that girdle the seedling and cause it to collapse — exactly what is visible here.

The desiccated, non-water-soaked appearance of the dead tissue strongly points to Rhizoctonia over the other damping-off pathogens.
